items.stem: During a chat, the user confirms that they want replies in Spanish from now on. Which memory tier should hold this?

options.text: Working context only.
options.feedback: Not enough. Working context is rebuilt every step, so the preference would be lost as soon as the step ends.

options.text: Session memory.
options.feedback: Too short-lived. Session memory ends with this conversation, but the user asked for the preference to apply from now on.

options.text: Long-term user memory, with its source and date.
options.feedback: Correct. It is a durable, confirmed fact about one user, so it belongs in long-term memory, scoped to that user and carrying its provenance.

options.text: Shared knowledge.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Shared knowledge is read by every user, so a personal preference stored there would leak and would apply to the wrong people.

items.explanation: Match each item to how long it should live and who may read it. A confirmed preference for one user is long-term memory, stored with where and when it was learned.

items.stem: Order these prompt sections from first to last so that the longest possible prefix can be prompt-cached.

items.text: The chunks retrieved for this turn's question.
The tool definitions, which change only on a release.
The system instructions, which change only on a release.
This user's long-term facts, which stay the same for the whole session.

items.explanation: A cache only helps for an unchanged prefix. Put the sections that change least often first, so the per-turn retrieval at the end never breaks the cached part.

items.stem: A long conversation has filled its 5,000-token history budget. This turn, retrieval used only 2,500 of its 4,000 tokens. What should happen to the history?

options.text: Let history borrow the 1,500 spare retrieval tokens for this turn.
options.feedback: Tempting but wrong. The next turn may need the full retrieval budget, and borrowing makes each section's size depend on the others.

options.text: Summarise or drop the oldest turns until history fits within 5,000 tokens.
options.feedback: Correct. Each section evicts within itself, so history shrinks its own content and every other budget stays fixed.

options.text: Drop the tool definitions to make room, since no tool may be needed.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That squeezes another section, breaks the cached prefix and may stop the model calling a tool it needs.

options.text: Expand the prompt to use the full 128,000-token window.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That abandons the budget and multiplies cost and latency for every later turn of the conversation.

items.explanation: Fixed section budgets keep cost predictable and stop one growing section from quietly degrading another. Eviction always happens inside the section that is full.

items.stem: A user asks whether the Pro plan includes phone support. None of the five retrieved chunks mentions phone support. What should the answer do?

options.text: Say yes, because premium plans usually include phone support.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is a claim with no source, drawn from the model's general knowledge, and it may be false for this product.

options.text: Say the help centre does not cover this, and offer a handover to a person.
options.feedback: Correct. No source, no claim. Saying not found is honest, and the handover still gets the user an answer.

options.text: Answer and cite the closest chunk, which describes Pro plan pricing.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A citation must support the claim it is attached to. Citing an unrelated chunk makes an unsupported answer look grounded.

options.text: Raise k to 50 and answer from whatever comes back.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That breaks the token budget, and more near-misses do not make the answer grounded.

items.explanation: Grounding means every claim is backed by a retrieved, cited chunk. When nothing supports an answer, the right output is not found, not a guess.

items.stem: Which belong in a grounded retrieval design? Select all that apply.

options.text: The number of chunks retrieved is bounded by a token budget.
options.feedback: Correct. A bounded read keeps the retrieval section within its share of the prompt.

options.text: Each chunk carries a source id and a timestamp.
options.feedback: Correct. The id makes citation possible, and the timestamp lets the answer prefer current material.

options.text: The answer cites the ids of the chunks it relies on.
options.feedback: Correct. Citations let readers and evaluators check each claim against its source.

options.text: The model fills gaps from general knowledge when no chunk matches.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That produces unsourced claims, which is exactly what grounding exists to prevent.

options.text: Whole documents are retrieved so that no context is ever missed.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Whole documents blow the token budget and bury the relevant passage among irrelevant text.

items.explanation: Grounded retrieval is bounded, sourced and cited. Anything the chunks do not support stays out of the answer.

items.stem: On 10 March an agent mistyped a customer's date of birth. The error was found and corrected on 24 March. An auditor asks what the system believed on 15 March. What does a bitemporal store return?

options.text: The corrected date, because that is the true value.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is what the system believes today. The auditor asked what it believed on 15 March, before the correction existed.

options.text: The mistyped date, because on 15 March it had not yet been superseded.
options.feedback: Correct. Querying as of 15 March sees only records made by then and not yet superseded, which is the mistyped one.

options.text: Nothing, because the mistyped record was deleted on 24 March.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A bitemporal store never deletes a record to correct it. The mistyped record is marked superseded and stays readable.

options.text: Both dates, and the auditor decides which applied.
options.feedback: Incorrect. An as-of query has one answer. On 15 March the correction had not been recorded, so it is not visible.

items.explanation: An as-of query filters by system time first. Only records made by the knowledge date and not yet superseded by then are visible.

items.stem: How does a bitemporal store apply a correction to a fact?

options.text: It updates the existing record in place.
options.feedback: Incorrect. An in-place update destroys the earlier belief, so past answers can no longer be explained or replayed.

options.text: It appends a new version and marks the old one superseded.
options.feedback: Correct. Both versions remain, each with its system time, so any past belief can be reproduced exactly.

options.text: It deletes the old record and inserts the new one.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Deleting loses history just as overwriting does, which defeats audits and replay.

options.text: It keeps both versions unmarked and lets the reader pick.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Without a superseded marker, the store cannot say which version it believed at a given moment.

items.explanation: Append and supersede is what makes as-of queries possible. Nothing is overwritten, and every record keeps the time it was made and the time it was replaced.

items.stem: An agent allows at most two retrieval attempts per question. Put the steps of a weak first attempt in order.

items.text: Grade the new chunks against the same relevance threshold.
Retrieve the top-k chunks for the user's question.
If the evidence is still weak, answer not found and offer a handover.
Rewrite the query and search a different source.
Grade each chunk for relevance and find too few pass.

items.explanation: Grade before answering, correct once, grade again, and stop at the bound. The fallback is an honest not found, never a third attempt.

items.stem: A corrective round adds 1.1 seconds, and 15 per cent of turns need one. Turns without one have a p95 of 5.2 seconds. The p95 target is 6 seconds. What follows?

options.text: Mean latency rises by only about 0.17 seconds, so the target is safe.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The mean rise is right, but the target is a p95. With 15 per cent of turns on the slow path, the p95 turn includes a corrective round.

options.text: The p95 turn now includes a corrective round, roughly 6.3 seconds, so the target is missed.
options.feedback: Correct. More than 5 per cent of turns take the slow path, so the tail carries the full 1.1 seconds. Shorten the round or the base path.

options.text: Remove grading so that no turn ever takes the corrective path.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That meets the latency target by answering from irrelevant chunks, trading a latency miss for wrong answers.

options.text: Allow unlimited corrective rounds but stop at 6 seconds.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A time cap is a bound, but the target would still be missed on the slow path, and unlimited rounds waste tokens before the cap.

items.explanation: A rare slow path barely moves the mean but sets the tail once it covers more than 5 per cent of turns. Budget the corrective round against p95, not the average.

items.stem: Which measures protect long-term user memory? Select all that apply.

options.text: Row-level security in the store, keyed on the calling user's id.
options.feedback: Correct. The store itself refuses to return another user's rows, whatever the prompt or model does.

options.text: A write policy accepting facts only from confirmed user statements or trusted systems.
options.feedback: Correct. It blocks memory poisoning from emails, documents and tool output.

options.text: A time-to-live on each fact.
options.feedback: Correct. Expiry limits how long a stale or poisoned fact can keep influencing sessions.

options.text: Deletion of every row under a user's id when they ask.
options.feedback: Correct. Deletion on request is a core obligation for memory that holds personal data.

options.text: A system prompt line telling the model to read only the current user's memories.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A prompt is not a control. One injection or bug can bypass it, so scope must live in the store.

options.text: Saving instructions found in retrieved documents as user preferences so they persist.
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is memory poisoning by design: untrusted text becomes a fact replayed in every later session.

items.explanation: Memory safety lives in the store and the write path. Scope reads by principal, guard writes by source, and let facts expire or be deleted on request.
